The proposed framework also introduces a new protocol to ensure the fairness of the trained models, preventing the central hub from exploiting the users for their own benefits. The scheme is built on the Security Games framework, analyzing the interactions between the users, the central hub, and potential attackers, demonstrating that the proposed framework is both computationally efficient and provably secure against malicious threats. The proposed framework is also demonstrated to be effective in real-world experiments, outperforming existing solutions in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Short-text categorization is a challenge due to the scarcity of discriminative information in short texts. To address this issue, this study examines how to leverage recent neural network models in short-text categorization. Our key findings indicate that both recurrent neural networks and convolutional neural networks are effective for short-text categorization. To further improve performance, this study proposes a novel neural network model that combines these two architectures by employing a recurrent neural network to capture sequential word dependencies and a convolutional neural network to extract word representations. Our proposed model is evaluated using a real-world microblogging dataset, achieving significant improvements over existing methods.

A telecentric resonator is essentially an optical device that combines the core principles of Fabry-Pérot etalons and confocal mirrors to produce multiple resonant frequencies. This unique device enables precise measurement of optical frequency differences through advanced telecentric resonators. This paper introduces an analytical model for telecentric resonators, focusing on the relationship between their free spectral range and physical dimensions, to better understand their potential applications.

A suitable pairing on a commutative group $G$ is defined as bijective map $G\times G\to G$ that remains invariant under simultaneous left and right multiplication of elements from $G$. The set $G$ itself is then a group under the operation resulting from the interaction of the group operation and the pairing function. In this research, a novel criterion for suitable pairings is proposed, and it is proven that this criterion has far-reaching implications in the realm of group-theory, resulting in significant findings such as the determination of the order of a group, and the identification of the dual group of a finite group. The work also extends to the context of algebraic groups, where the existence of nontrivial Cartan subgroups is established, and a generalization of the Levi-Malcev theorem is proved for suitable pairings.

The development and deployment of custom-built computing systems are increasingly driven by the integration of specialized "chiplet" components, particularly in high-performance applications. This trend is gaining momentum in fields such as machine learning, high-energy physics, and quantum computing. However, the complexity of these systems is exacerbated by the need for efficient communication between diverse hardware components. This research explores the potential of using codelets - compact code segments - to simplify the process of deploying chiplet-based systems, and proposes the Codelet Framework as a software architecture to support this effort. The study also identifies the key challenges and non-functional requirements that must be addressed in this new paradigm.

A novel approach is introduced to estimate a mixture cure model, which is particularly effective in the presence of right-censored data and heavy-tailed response variables. The estimation procedure is conducted via maximum conditional likelihood estimation, however, conventional estimation methods are hindered by the nonidentifiability of the model parameters when the covariates exhibit collinearity. A new method of parameter estimation is presented to resolve this issue, which involves a two-stage approach. In the first stage, the conditional distribution of the responses given covariates is estimated, followed by the estimation of the conditional distribution of the failure times, conditional on covariates and response values. A smoothed estimator is then employed to obtain an initial consistent estimator of the remaining parameters. A second-stage maximum conditional likelihood estimator is subsequently derived, based on a re-estimation of the conditional distributions from the initial stage. Theoretical results are established to demonstrate the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimation method, which is further supported by simulation studies and an empirical application.

We introduce the one-dimensional nonlocal distance graph property and examine its connections to metric dimension and nonlocal distance dimension. Specifically, we establish that a nonlocal distance graph of dimension less than 2 is equivalent to having a diameter of 1. Moreover, for any graph G, the minimum diameter is bounded by the difference between the diameter and the diameter of its quotient graph divided by a constant, and the difference between the metric dimension and the nonlocal distance dimension.

Modern computing systems are transitioning to in-memory computing (IMC) to achieve exceptional performance in AI, big data analytics, and machine learning. However, the memory-access based programming model introduces new security risks, including memory access side-channel attacks that leak sensitive data. To address this concern, this paper investigates the security of three prominent IMC frameworks - DaMem, Memcached, and Intel Optane DC DAX, evaluating their vulnerability to memory access side-channel attacks. Our research reveals that Memcached and DaMem are susceptible to SMT timing and memory bypass attacks, revealing their memory access behavior. In contrast, Intel Optane DC DAX, with its PMEM protection mechanism, proved to be secure against these attacks.

We suggest a set of simplified polarization kernels that facilitate the computation of the two-dimensional cross-correlation polarization response function. The polarization kernel is defined as the convolution of the two-dimensional cross-correlation response function and the polarization structure function. By approximating the polarization structure function as a Taylor series expansion, we derived analytical expressions for the polarization kernels that significantly reduce computational complexity without sacrificing accuracy. Specifically, these simplified kernels yield a reduction in the number of required measurements by N times, allowing for an overall computational cost reduction of N times, assuming each measurement takes T seconds. The new expression for the polarization kernel also enables the precise determination of the measurement's uncertainty, whereas the traditional approach necessitate N separate measurements for an equivalent uncertainty assessment.

Seismic noise, often introduced by nearby human activities, hinders the accurate analysis of seismic waves and limits the capabilities of earthquake location and waveform interpretation. Seismic data are frequently contaminated at specific locations, notably at coastal and industrial zone boundaries, where noise and signal are measured simultaneously. Conventional noise filtering techniques, based on frequency domain analysis, are often ineffective in removing noise from complex seismic data. A new transfer learning-based method is presented, capable of autonomously identifying and eliminating noise from a target area, without relying on a noise reference. By leveraging the differences in frequency domain characteristics between noise and signal sections, derived from nearby areas with known noise patterns, the proposed approach achieves significant noise reduction. Numerical simulations, utilizing real seismic data collected from a coal mine in China, demonstrate the effectiveness of the introduced transfer learning-based noise removal technique.

The study of electron- and positron scattering off protons serves as a crucial tool in understanding the structure of both the proton and nucleon electromagnetic current. However, existing experimental research on this topic has been hindered by the limitations of available data, particularly in terms of the missing momentum's magnitude. To address this issue, we have conducted a comprehensive numerical analysis of elastic electron-proton, positron-proton, electron-proton with real photon emission, and positron-proton with real photon emission using the relativistic quantum electrodynamics model. Our results show that the average squared values of the transferred momentum's components and the scattering angle are significantly influenced by the initial lepton's mass and the direction of its initial and final momenta. We have also found that the asymmetry in momentum transfer is a valuable indicator of the nucleon's electroweak structure in the context of the vector dominance model. Furthermore, our study reveals that the average values of lepton and antilepton energies are primarily determined by the photon's emission process. To make our findings more applicable to experimental research, we have developed a set of semi-analytical formulas for calculating various parameters, such as lepton and photon average energies, photon emission probabilities, photon average energy, and photon emission direction distribution.

We have conducted a theoretical study on the electronic properties of a 2$D$ Hubbard model incorporating a specific spin-orbit interaction, which is inspired by the electronic properties of a 4$d$ transition metal oxide, such as Sr$_2$IrO$_4$.  In this model, a Fermi-singlet state is favored at zero temperature.  However, spin-orbit interaction causes the formation of bound states that result in a ladder-like spectrum.  In this study, we examine the electronic properties of a STM tip as it scans the surface of a Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ material, accounting for the finite temperature and tip-sample interaction.  We found that the spectrum of Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ is characterized by a series of closely-spaced bound states near the Fermi level.  We propose that the observation of these bound states by STM in Sr$_2$Irso$_4$ materials can be used to validate the presence of spin-polaron ladders in this material.

In a clinical trial assessing a medication's impact via different factors, researchers aim to identify the treatment's relationship with the outcome through an intermediate step. A recent study developed an assessment framework called multiply robust mediated conditions to confirm treatment effects in real-world scenarios, particularly for non-normal treatment data. However, this study aims to enhance this framework by validating treatment validity using various types of data and mediating processes, including binary, categorical, continuous, or multiple mixed types. The researchers introduce a new concept of multiply sturdy conditions, which combines different types of data and mediating processes to verify treatment validity. The study demonstrates that these conditions can be created from various data sources and proves that confirming multiple robust conditions reliably establishes the treatment's impact. Simulation studies demonstrate that this framework is effective in different scenarios and compares it to existing methods like semiparametric mediation analysis and a conventional regression-based approach. The study's findings confirm the effectiveness of the treatment in a real-world trial on type 2 diabetes patients.

This particular issue of New Astronomy is a dedicated compilation of research focused on starshades - devices employed to block starlight in an interferometric setup, thereby enabling high-sensitivity observations of faint celestial objects at various wavelengths, especially in the infrared spectrum. The issue serves as a perfect complement to an earlier ASA/NASPA "Unobscured Stars" Meeting held in 2017, as part of the "Unblotted Stars" series. This editorial introduces the issue and provides an informative overview of the field through a set of illustrations and key observations.

A substantial number of individuals die by suicide annually, with approximately 800,000 suicides globally, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk populations and detecting early suicidal behavior. While online behavior can help identify suicidal risk factors, distinguishing between phrases indicative of suicidal intent and benign language remains a significant challenge. The "I will if you just stop eating and won't eat at all I'll kill myself" kind of phrase may be misinterpreted as suicidal or threatening from a linguistic perspective, yet it is not a cry for help. The complexities of detecting suicidal language have been studied, but existing datasets lack diversity in suicidal behavior, failing to provide a comprehensive understanding. In an effort to address this gap, a new dataset called Robin was created by compiling suicidal and off-ludicrous labels and associated text from Reddit. This dataset will facilitate the advancement of research in detecting suicidal language, serving as a benchmark for public release.

A brief examination is given to a hypothetical black hole cosmology, characterized by super-vacuum properties, though this analysis is primarily exploratory in nature. The primary objective of this study involves determining the (super)potential tensors corresponding to this cosmological context, which is often referred to as a'super' version of the blackian mechanics principle. The research also involves a discussion on the stability aspects of this particular cosmological context.

This study examines the long-term behavior of solutions to a difference equation. The initial findings were applied to a model of tumor growth, which is represented by a nonlinear equation specifically analyzing bone tumor growth following the application of radiotherapy. The solution's bounds were initially determined using a generalized variation of constants formula, and subsequent findings established bounds on tumor size over an infinite period. The equation's long-term behavior was also investigated by converting it into a nonlinear differential equation, and the space mapping method was used to generalize the findings to a nonlinear differential equation. The study then returned to the context of bone tumor growth, leveraging the established bounds on tumor size over an infinite period to suggest a potential radiotherapy treatment strategy.

A group of theories based on the Born-Infeld model of electrodynamics is examined, where an additional scalar field is included. The scalar field interacts with the magnetic field through a Yukawa-type interaction, which in turn generates a Chern-Simons term when integrated. With the addition of a charged scalar field, the theory's neutrality is ensured. The inclusion of a cosmological constant allows for asymptotically flat or de Sitter black hole solutions to be formed. The presence of a positive cosmological constant results in an anti-de Sitter black hole, while the inclusion of a massless scalar field leads to an extreme black hole. The analysis is extended to include a set of generalizations, where the theory remains consistent and the inclusion of a positive cosmological constant results in an extreme black hole. The extreme black hole has horizons that are null hypersurfaces. The non-linear nature of the Born-Infeld electrodynamics leads to a set of regular black hole solutions, where an electric charge parameter is present. The presence of a de Sitter cosmological constant results in an anti-de Sitter black hole, which also exhibits an event horizon that is a null hypersurface. The extreme black hole has a co-axial asymptote. The analysis is extended to a set of theories where the Born-Infeld electric field is coupled to a set of scalar fields, which also leads to a non-linear electrodynamics. The inclusion of a Chern-Simons term leads

A subset $\mathcal{S}$ of a free monoid $F^*$, where the monoid is generated by a finite set $F$, is considered a Karamata Sidon collection if every element in $\mathcal{S}$ has a distinct number of factors of prime divisors, as well as if the sum of the prime divisor counts for each element in $\mathcal{S}$ equals the size of the set $\mathcal{S}$. This work focuses on determining the size of the largest Sidon collections for words in the linear expression form of the monoid $F^*$, specifically when the set $F$ consists of $n$ distinct elements. It is shown that the size of the largest Sidon collection is bounded by $O(n^{3n/4})$ and is determined for specific cases. The size of Sidon collections is also calculated for special types of linear expressions in the monoid $F^*$, specifically when the set $F$ consists of a single prime number and its powers.

In the quantum XY chain, the phase transition zone is affected by temperature at absolute zero. By employing exact diagonalization and renormalization group methods, we investigate the magnetic susceptibility near the critical phase transition zone and observe the application of finite-temperature scaling in the quantum XY chain. Furthermore, we identify the critical exponent ν, utilizing magnetization and spatial phase characteristics. Utilizing these exponents, we establish a scaling function for the magnetic susceptibility, and by comparing it to the scaling function for the specific heat, we discover that both exhibit the same critical exponent ν. Additionally, we establish a scaling function for the spatial phase transition boundary, and by comparing it to the one derived from the quantum Potts chain, we verify that both share the same critical exponent ν.

Theoretical studies on the Ising model's behavior near the critical point have been conducted, focusing on the impact of a third-order transition. Results from these studies suggested that a hotter system should cool more quickly to equilibrium. Contrary to expectations, our Monte Carlo simulations indicate that a ferromagnetic phase evolving at lower temperatures actually takes longer to reach equilibrium than one evolving at higher temperatures.

We examine the motion of two particles within a one-dimensional power-law quasicrystal under a specific potential, with their movement influenced by power-law correlated hopping. By using the power exponent $ \alpha $, we demonstrate that for any value of $\alpha$ between 0 and 1, a stable two-particle state exists at a specific distance from the quasicrystal, with this distance decreasing as $\alpha$ approaches 1. Furthermore, we show that for any value of $\alpha$ above 1, these two particles can become localized at an increasingly smaller distance as $\alpha$ increases. This research establishes a new class of one-dimensional quasicrystals where the motion of two particles can be controlled through manipulation of $\alpha$.

Recent years have seen numerous advancements in Multilingual Task-Focused Dialogue (MTFD) systems, which enable computers to engage in more efficient interactions with humans. These dialogue systems, which are typically used in customer service settings, can now support interactions across language barriers, thanks to the integration of Multilingual Intent Detection (MID) and Multilingual Slot Detection (MSD) models. However, the development of MTFD systems across diverse languages remains a significant challenge, particularly when resources are scarce. In this paper, we examine the existing body of literature on MTFD systems, highlighting the existing trade-offs between resource availability and language diversity, and identify areas for improvement to bridge the gap between languages and advance the state-of-the-art research in this field.

The regulation of alternative splicing is crucial for maintaining cellular regulation and modifying disease progression. Although the regulation of alternative splicing is still not fully understood, we investigated short-term fluctuations in brain splicing by examining short-duration changes in gene expression. We discovered that a significant portion of genes, approximately one-third, exhibit rapid and variable splicing dynamics, suggesting that alternative splicing is dynamically regulated over short periods. Furthermore, we found that brain cells express a large number of alternative splicings, with estimates suggesting that every gene produces tens to thousands of variant transcripts. We also observed that differential splicing is influenced by the degree of alternative splicing and the rate of mRNA decay, and we found that a large proportion of genes exhibit short-term fluctuations in gene expression due to both transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms. The results suggest that alternative splicing is dynamically regulated over short periods.

The privacy laws and technical standards for handling personal data are intricate and subject to change as new technologies emerge. As a result, organizations face difficulties in complying with these regulations, particularly when implementing cutting-edge technologies that require substantial custom-made software development. This research explores the ways in which data privacy compliance challenges manifest during software development, particularly in the context of implementing technical privacy measures. Our qualitative study of technical professionals' experiences identified key insights into their experiences and practical suggestions for improving software development to enhance data privacy adherence. This guidance encompasses strategies to facilitate collaboration among technical and non-technical staff, the creation of shared resources, and the incorporation of privacy considerations into software development methodologies.

In the initial stages of relativistic $pA$ collisions, where multiple collisions occur, we examine how two and more particle patterns in the transverse plane form at an early stage. Our findings indicate that directional correlations among particles, similar to those observed in $AA$ collisions, become apparent, provided the particles' path can be tracked long enough. These correlations are influenced by the first significant interaction and, as such, they can serve as indicators for each individual collision. Moreover, we discovered that the presence of a target nucleus causes a shift in the pattern of these directional correlations, resulting in asymmetry. This asymmetry, in turn, reveals information about the number of collisions and, more specifically, it provides insight into how angular dependences of each individual collision evolve.

The origin of light nuclei in heavy ion collisions is studied through a statistical model simulation, where interactions between protons, neutrons, and $\alpha$ particles below 2.0 GeV are taken into account. A simulation of an Au-Au collision at 3 GeV centre-of-mass energy was performed to examine light nuclei production. Diverse coalescence mechanisms contribute to this process, and a coalescence ratio of (p, $\alpha$, $^{4}$He) is calculated for various transverse momentum and collision centrality conditions. This coalescence ratio is then compared to similar data obtained from the STAR experiment. A correlation between the coalescence ratio, collision centrality, and mass of the produced particles is observed. A coalescence ratio of (p, $\alpha$, $^{4}$He) is also calculated for a more asymmetric collision system, Be-Be, at the same centre-of-mass energy. A comparison between the two collision systems reveals a similar coalescence ratio, but with the Be-Be data showing a more pronounced mass dependence.

The NASA Architecture Analysis Program's assessment of future space missions
provides valuable input in identifying the suitable planetary environments for
the ongoing search for life on distant planets. This analysis will focus on the
categories of exoplanets that are considered promising candidates for the
search for habitable environments, both inside and outside the planets' habitable
zones. These include rocky exoplanets with Earth-like atmospheres, those with
cooler atmospheres, and small, rocky exoplanets with thin atmospheres. This study
will also examine existing mission concepts that are targeted for the search for
planets in these categories, the instruments and data required to study their
atmospheres, and their suitability for long-term observation and follow-up.

We establish the existence of a solvable circulant graph with confinality of three, given certain conditions on the set of host numbers. Additionally, the case where the set of host numbers equals the set of prime numbers is explored in detail.

This paper presents an enhanced version of the Rapid Iterative Matrix Inversion (RIMI) algorithm, initially developed by Beltrame, Griesshammer, and Stevenson, designed for parallel computing on GPU clusters. The existing algorithm's convergence rate is not sufficient for achieving fast calculations within the timeframes required for the STEREO-B mission. To address this limitation, the authors have introduced a novel approach, referred to as Elevated Order RIMI (EORIMI), which enhances the convergence speed by utilizing higher-order iterative solutions. EORIMI's performance is demonstrated through the successful simulation of the STEREO-B mission's requirements, resulting in a significant improvement in the required 0.1-second response time. The authors have also explored the potential for further enhancements through the consideration of multiple iterative solutions in parallel, as well as the application of finite-field arithmetic, to facilitate real-time processing.

We examine the influence of back reaction on ultra-slow-roll inflation, focusing on its effects during slow-roll and deep ultra-sslow-roll phases, to determine when power spectrum amplification occurs. Our analysis reveals that the power spectrum enhancement resulting from back reaction differs from previous findings, especially in slow-roll scenarios, where it's considered minimal. However, a significant boost in power spectrum is observed when inflation transitions from slow-roll to deep ultra-slow-roll phases, due to an amplification of tensor modes.

We investigated a complex mathematical problem known as the Enhanced Selection Optimization Problem, which deals with the efficient distribution of limited resources. These resources need to be allocated across a range of options while meeting specific requirements for each, and their optimal arrangement should also meet overall quality standards. Our research focused on finding the most suitable allocation strategy that meets all these conditions, with an emphasis on maximizing the total quality achieved. We developed a new mathematical framework that allows for a more efficient analysis of this issue, and our results include insights into the nature of this problem and some strategies for addressing it. Furthermore, our findings show that this issue is particularly challenging to solve computationally, and we were able to develop an algorithm that can provide guaranteed solutions for it.

The majority of statistical models are based on the assumption that the underlying data follows a distribution with non-event outcome probabilities being constant across observation periods. However, this common model scenario often proves inadequate in real-world scenarios where participants experience events over time, particularly in settings where the probability of an event varies based on accumulated exposure or the duration between events. To address this limitation, we introduce an alternative framework for analyzing time-to-event data that is grounded in probability theory, drawing inspiration from the concept of causal case baseline in epidemiology. Our approach is based on the probability of an event occurring during a specified time interval following a prior event, with the objective of estimating this interval probability using historical data and applying it to new cases to determine the expected number of events within that interval. By doing so, our framework offers a direct comparison of the likelihood of events occurring within different time intervals, without necessitating the estimation of complex models. Moreover, we demonstrate that our method is sensitive to changes in event probabilities in response to prior events, and that it can be adapted to account for additional covariates and models for varying event probabilities.

High-precision calculations in particle physics necessitate precise determination of Feynman integrals.  Due to the emergence of new physics beyond the Standard Model, accurate computations are vital for accurately determining their properties.  In this study, we examine the feasibility of representing generic two-loop Feynman integrals with massless propagands and single massive external particles using the most precise mathematical formulas.  We utilize the BZ-expansion, which can be calculated to an arbitrary level of precision, to verify the accuracy of these mathematical representations.  By comparing the results to those obtained using the most precise computational methods, we found that the precise mathematical formulas can be used to a level of precision of $10^{-8}$.  Furthermore, we found that the BZ-expansion is effective up to a scale of $10^{-3}$, which is comparable to the scale associated with the Higgs boson mass.  In light of these results, we suggest that the most precise mathematical formulas be used to represent generic two-loop integrals with massless propagands and single massive external particles.

The performance of the Lustre system was compared to DAOS for managing object data in two different approaches. By integrating a new Lustre client and client/server interface into the existing code, two distinct Lustre-based object data management systems were developed. One is an object-based system that uses object-based metadata to store metadata and data together, while the other uses a separate metadata store. These systems were thoroughly tested and optimized for optimal performance. Similarly, two object-based data management systems were developed using the Lustre file system to store metadata and data, one with explicit metadata and the other with meta-data tags. For comparison purposes, the same data sets were used for all four systems in this study. Performance metrics including read and write rates, data throughput, I/O efficiency, metadata management, and data management were evaluated and compared. Performance analysis revealed that systems based on meta-data tagging performed better than those with separate metadata stores, especially when handling data with high metadata content. Systems based on DAOS performed better than those based on Lustre, with the former outperforming the latter by significant margins in read and write rates, data throughput, and metadata management efficiency during initial tests. However, the scenario involving high metadata content showed similar performance from both DAOS and Lustre-based systems. Further research could explore the use of tag-based metadata systems to improve performance.

The rapid expansion of electric vehicles on the roads is accompanied by increasing demands from drivers to utilize charging infrastructure, particularly while parked, thereby generating revenue for landlords through rental fees and tolls. However, to meet this need and prevent overoccupation of parking spaces, a digital system for managing vehicle access and parking spot allocation is proposed. The proposed system optimizes parking space utilization and ensures that the vehicle can complete its charging session within the allotted time. Upon arrival, the system facilitates vehicle parking, sets a departure time, and sends notifications to the driver to depart on schedule. By optimizing parking duration, this system enables more vehicles to use the same parking spot, thereby increasing facility revenue and reducing congestion. To address the needs of both facility owners and drivers, this research explores the problem of optimizing parking space utilization under varying driver preferences. The problem is formulated as a location-based routing problem, where it involves determining the optimal parking location and departure time. To solve this complex issue, a two-stage integer programming model is developed, where the first stage locates the optimal parking location, and the second stage determines the departure time. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a case study and a simulation study using real-world data.

This article establishes the concept of LCD codes and demonstrates their inherent independence from field characteristics. Building upon this foundation, it introduces a condition for the non-degenerate sum of two linear codes, and as a result, derives the existence of optimal LCD codes with specific parameters for the finite fields $\mathbb{F}_{q}$, $\mathbf{F}_{q^2}$, and $\mathbf{F}_{q^3}$. Moreover, it investigates linear codes of arbitrary dimensions and minimum distance two from the extended finite fields $\mathbf{F}_{q^m}\left[x;\,\theta\right]$, where m is at least 3 and θ is a θ is an arbitrary a root of unity.

We demonstrate that loop momentum integrations can generate a standard gravitational potential, such as $1/r$, despite the latter does not arise from tree-level calculations under dimensional regularization.

A massive transition to renewable energy is underway across the western United States, transitioning away from fossil fuels to address climate change. This shift poses a complex problem, as it requires the integration of diverse land-based resources, such as solar power generation, to meet growing electricity demands while minimizing environmental and social impacts. This study presents a comprehensive model that balances the decarbonization of six western states - California, Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, and Colorado - with the utilization of land for both renewable energy development and conservation purposes. By simulating various scenarios, we assess the impact of different assumptions on the environmental and social costs of this transition, including habitat loss, fragmentation, and land fragmentation, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the numerous factors influencing the conversion to renewable energy.

Cluster randomized trials are frequently utilized to evaluate the efficacy of vaccines by grouping similar subjects within the same cluster, thereby assessing the impact of the intervention on the individual along with any surrounding participants. Estimating the intervention's effect on the subjects while accounting for the within-cluster correlation among treatment groups presents a significant challenge. This analysis seeks to define relevant estimands under standard assumptions and determine suitable analysis techniques for assessing these estimands.

We introduce a novel fractal method for creating plane Octagonal Networks, utilizing M\"{o}bius transformations that preserve a specific geometric constraint. We analyze the Laplacian spectra of these networks, derived from standardized adjacency matrices. Notably, the eigenvalue distribution exhibits both bounded and unbounded intervals. Our investigation also encompasses the Laplacian spectra of larger, non-fractal Octagonal Networks, including the 16-vertex generalized Octagonal Network. We establish a connection between the Laplacian spectra of these networks and their associated vertex-disjoint $k$-paths. We further explore the Laplacian Spectra in the context of real-world systems, including the human brain's (3,4)-skeleton.

In a two-player game, we examine how two agents, connected through a shared context, can learn from each other's actions. These agents make simultaneous, independent decisions based on the current state, and their payoffs depend on both the state and the actions taken. We consider a scenario where the actions are determined by a known, context-dependent matrix and the rewards are fully observable. We focus on a setting where the actions are public information, and the players' moves are observed by the other player. We propose a model-free, model-free, zero-sum contextual linear bandit algorithm that allows each player to determine an optimal action based on the current state. We establish a regret bound for this algorithm and demonstrate that it is possible to achieve this bound even if the players do not share the context. We also present a lower bound on the regret, showing that our algorithm's performance is optimal.

Digital health records are being used more frequently for various research and clinical purposes. However, they often contain sensitive information that necessitates anonymization, which is why we're developing a method to create synthetic datasets. This paper focuses on constructing a synthetic cystic fibrosis patient cohort, incorporating both clinical data and sensor readings to simulate a real-world scenario involving a patient's interaction with a clinical environment and medical equipment. Our approach incorporates a probability distribution calculator, utilizing Gaussian mixture models and conditional copula models. We've also derived a set of underlying governing equations to facilitate the computation of these distributions. Experimental results show that our synthesized data exhibits strong similarity to the original digital health records, as evidenced by the low Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances between the two.

Researchers have analyzed the decay processes of $D^0$ mesons into various combinations of kaons and pions using proton-proton collisions at the LHCb. The data were gathered at collision energies of $7$, $8$, and $13\,\text{TeV}$, corresponding to accumulated luminosities of $2$, $9.8$, and $9.4$ fb$^{-1}$ respectively. The investigation focused on the three-body decay modes of $D^0$ mesons into $K^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$, $K^+\pi^-\pi^+\pi^+$, and $K^+\pi^2\pi^-$, and used a partial reconstruction technique to identify the $K^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^+$ final state. The study confirmed the presence of known $D^0$ resonances, including the $\overline{K}^0(794)^0$, $D_s(2715)^+$, and $D_s(2860)^{0,(-)}$, in addition to the newly observed $D^0(2550)^-$ and $D^0(2500)^-$ and the previously known $D^0(2430)^-$ isospin partners. The study's results were compared to the findings of previous experiments, and the analysis of the $K^-\pi^2\pi^-$ final state revealed the presence

Our team recently developed Novelpy, a Python library for analyzing original and disruptiveness in citation networks and scientific literature. By building on existing knowledge, we created a comprehensive tool that combines various approaches, including citation measures, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the originality and impact of scientific publications. The Novelpy library is available for open-source use under the MIT License and can be freely accessed on GitHub.

Laser pulses can be incredibly powerful, but their effectiveness is often limited by the damage they cause to optical components, making it difficult to achieve the desired outcome in a complex system involving various lasers working together. To address this issue, researchers have developed a system where multiple lasers are connected in a way that allows for a range of possibilities. By carefully adjusting the interaction between different laser beams, it's possible to create a range of dynamic laser patterns, from simple to complex, that can be used to manipulate multiple lasers working at the same frequency, or a large group of lasers working at different frequencies. This innovation opens up new possibilities for the development of powerful lasers that can be used in a variety of applications, from space exploration to quantum information processing.

A long-standing fascination with archery, a timeless challenge for humans, has
given rise to a variety of targeted AI applications within this field. These complex
tasks, such as calculating optimal trajectories and target selection, are crucial
within the realm of Recurve Archery. To bridge the gap between AI advancements
and real-world archery capabilities, a novel research approach was developed, where
AI-generated shots were simulated within a virtual environment. By utilizing a
specialized game engine, a virtual archery set was created, encompassing a virtual
bow, targets, and environment. Our preliminary findings detail the process of
setting up the simulation, achieving accurate trajectory predictions, and the
outcomes of our initial experiments. The ultimate goal of this project, dubbed
"AutoBow," is to design a machine that can fire a real bow, in a controlled
setting, in an effort to closely match the simulations' predictions.

The cross-domain recommendation task involves predicting a user's preferences on a target domain by utilizing information from a source domain where the user's preferences are well-documented.  Historically, this task has been approached by either transferring user and item embeddings directly through neural networks or by transferring latent user and item representations.  A novel approach presented in this paper is to simultaneously learn two distinct metric spaces - one suitable for embedding target domain information and the other for embedding source domain information.  This dual approach is demonstrated to yield superior results over traditional methods involving the direct transfer of embeddings or the transfer of latent representations.  Additionally, this paper introduces a streamlined neural network architecture that efficiently incorporates the dual metric spaces and requires fewer model parameters than typical approaches.  The proposed architecture's efficiency and performance superiority are empirically verified using several benchmark datasets.

We present a segment-based characterization of the modal mu-calculus for distributed systems, where the segment utilized is the conc-MSO monad. As a result, this demonstrates that the modal mu-language's expressiveness remains unchanged when transitioning from a linear to a concurrent model. Furthermore, our work involves defining a characterization of the concMSO monad through a linear segment-based approach.

Our investigation focuses on thermal exchange within a two-dimensional plasma torus that is sustained by a heated plasma source. This torus is modeled as a two-dimensional, axisymmetric object, with its density and temperature being influenced by the radial position. We have found that thermal diffusion is primarily driven by the density gradient, with less significant contributions from the temperature gradient. We have developed a set of equations to describe this process and have identified the critical parameters that govern them. By applying these equations, we are able to accurately predict the observed temperature distributions within the plasma torus.

We examine linear combinations of unsorted sets of numerical data. These combinations can be viewed as a type of kernel that acknowledges the internal structure of the data set. To begin, we investigate the geometric properties of these combinations and reveal that they form a closed set within a space defined by the maximum and minimum values of the linear mixtures. Subsequently, we establish a method to determine whether a specific value is attainable within this closed set. Additionally, we consider the task of approximating a target value using linear combinations, providing a solution through the construction of an associated normal distribution, whose mean and variance enable us to define an efficient and effective search range for the approximating value.

Cardiac angiography, a minimally invasive treatment for coronary artery disease, involves injecting contrast medium into the heart's blood vessels through catheters, utilizing X-ray imaging to capture the arteries' silhouettes. The procedure's success relies heavily on the experienced operator's skill, particularly in minimizing radiation exposure. In this study, a deep learning-based approach is proposed to optimize X-ray radiation use in cardio-angiography, aiming to enhance image quality while reducing the operator's need for manual adjustments. A deep convolutional neural network is trained to predict optimal X-ray exposure settings based on the vessel silhouettes and camera angles, allowing the network to generate optimal exposure adjustments or recommend the best camera angles for improved image quality. In experiments using real-world data, the proposed method demonstrates significant reductions in X-ray exposure by two to three times in cardio-angiography, showcasing its potential to support operators in minimizing radiation use while maintaining excellent diagnostic quality.

We examine the prospects and hurdles associated with the creation of charmonium and bottomonium states at a higher-energy $e^+e^-$ collider, specifically the FCC-ee, focusing on the production of these states in $e^+e^-$ collisions. The study of heavy-flavor physics is highly valued at FCC-ee and plays a crucial role in the analysis of its physics program, offering significant contributions, for example, precise measurements of the $Z^0$ boson's transition matrix elements and examination of the strong interaction's non-perturbative regime. The production of charmonium and bottomonium states in $e^+e^-$ collisions enables the investigation of the heavy-flavor quarkonia's temperature-dependent behavior in the hot quark gluon plasma, a crucial aspect of the study of the hot QCD. The production of charmonium and bottomonium states also offers a means to determine the $e^+e^-$ annihilation cross sections, a vital component in the analysis of the physics at FCC-ee. The investigation of the heavy-flavor physics at FCC-ee is highly complex and poses various challenges, including the analysis of the heavy-flavor quarkonia's production and the decay of the heavy-flavor hadrons.

Lepton number conservation by a $U(1)$ gauge symmetry, which only preserves
electron number, is a common feature in many models that attempt to explain
neutrino mass generation. This symmetry is often associated with a 'barrier'
that prevents chargeless fermions from forming a dark matter component, due to
the continuous variation of lepton flavors. In this study, we examine the
effect of the $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ symmetry on this 'barrier'. Our
results show that even when the symmetry is broken, a significant portion of
dark matter can still be formed from transformed neutrinos. This is because
the symmetry only allows lepton number to vary as $\Delta L_3 = \Delta L_0 +
\Delta L_z$, where $\Delta L_3$ is the total lepton number and $\Delta L_z
= -\mu_\tau$, $\mu_\tau$ is a gauge charge. This altered symmetry causes the
mass spectrum of charged lepton flavor violating processes to be different from
the original $U(1)_{L_{e}}$ symmetry.

The evolution of stellar clusters and galaxies is significantly influenced by dynamical processes and their surroundings. The effect of external influences on stellar clusters and substructures within the Milky Way is well understood in the context of dynamical friction, tidal forces, and tidal disruption. However, the impact of secular perturbations due to companion stars and their implications on the internal structure of stellar clusters and substructures have not been fully explored. In this study, we investigate the effects of secular perturbations on stellar clusters and hypervelocity stars. We simulate the evolution of stellar clusters with an intermediate-mass companion (0.1-10 solar masses) using the N-body code REBound, taking into account the effect of a companion's secular perturbation on the cluster's orbit and internal structure. The results show that this perturbation causes a gradual increase in the cluster's eccentricity, leading to a significant expansion of the cluster's half-mass radius. The observed expansion is comparable to that caused by dynamical friction, but the effect is cumulative and long-lasting. The effect of a companion's perturbation on the cluster's orbital energy is also significant, leading to ejection of stars with energies exceeding the cluster's binding energy, which become hypervelocity stars. The simulations show that a stellar cluster with a mass of 10 solar masses and a companion mass of 0.1 solar masses can produce hypervelocity stars within a few billion years. We prove that the solution of a multiplicative stochastic differential equation with singular drift terms can be expressed as the limit of solutions to analogous equations with modified drift terms, provided the modified drifts meet certain criteria. These'modified' equations are well-defined and exhibit some regularity. By proving the existence and uniqueness of solutions to these modified equations, we demonstrate the existence of 'feeble' solutions to the original singular multiplicative SDE. This research builds upon existing techniques for studying stochastic differential equations with singular drifts across multiple fields, including the works of Da Lio, Zambotti, Ryzhov-Oskolkov, and others.

The situation with regards to the definability of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ in all uncountable cardinalities $\kappa$ is explored. It is shown that in a $\kappa$-complete ultrafilter $U$ on $\omega_1$, the ideal $\NS[\omega_1]$ can be uniquely defined if and only if $U$ is a $F_\sigma$-point, which is a result with far-reaching implications. Additionally, it is established that in a certain class of inner models, specifically those within the $L$-hierarchy, the definability of $\NS[\omega_1]$ leads to the definability of the random ideal on $\omega_1$. Furthermore, it is shown that in these models, the use of a $\Sigma^1_2$-covering lemma in a $\Sigma^1_2$-sequence has a significant impact on its properties. These findings have implications for both the $J(\omega_1)$-hierarchy and the $L$-hierarchy, specifically for inner models within these hierarchies.

The effectiveness of objectives for adjusting pre-trained language models is assessed.
A customized framework, called Adaptor, facilitates objective adjustment by utilizing an objective transformer as a framework and object adjustment as a method.
Language model adaptability is evaluated by adjusting the model to suit a new objective without modifying the original model.
A comprehensive study was conducted to compare different objective adjustment approaches for enhancing various language tasks.
Adjusting language models to different objectives notably improves the performance of models on multiple tasks and data combinations.
Adjusting models to suitable objectives yields better results than fine-tuning on specific data.
A notable improvement is seen in models adjusting to objectives at a faster pace than fine-tuning on specific tasks.

A large database of street images called Mapillary has been used to collect and analyze data from around the world. This global collaboration, involving contributors from over 183 countries, has amassed more than 8.4 million images by the end of 2020. The majority of these images are traffic signs, which are the focus of a new study that utilizes a novel framework for identification and classification. The proposed approach combines a novel cost function with a robust optimization algorithm to effectively classify traffic signs from the Mapillary dataset. The study also highlights the benefits of using the Mapillary platform for data collection and its key features that make it well-suited for machine learning applications in this context. The study's experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

To improve recommendation accuracy and reduce operational costs, self-supervised learning has become a promising approach within collaborative filtering. Although many self-supervised methods for recommendation rely on self-attention mechanisms, these methods often overlook the importance of user and item similarities. Building on this concept, we propose a novel self-supervised framework called SelfCF, which incorporates collaborative structures through graph augmentation and employs self-supervision to enhance user and item representations. To facilitate efficient training, SelfCF can be seamlessly integrated with existing self-supervised methods and conventional methods without requiring additional training or hyperparameter adjustments. Thorough experiments demonstrate that SelfCF significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, achieving a significant increase in recall and NDCG of 10.8% and 16.4% respectively.

We define the $k$th degree universal Tevelev levels as $\mathbb{P}^1(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ with divisors of degree $k$. These levels form a Hodge structure, and we find that they are rational for $k\ge5$ and torsion for $k\ge7$ up to isomorphism. We also find that the Tate twists of the $k$th degree universal Tevelev levels are generated by a specific morphism for $k\ge5$.

This research presents a novel Dirac semimetal model, characterized by both linear and parabolic dispersion patterns, which we hypothesize is stable within a defined phase. A gapped Dirac model was previously introduced by a different author [Phys. Rev. B 99, 165407 (2019)]. To further analyze its properties, we employed a second-order perturbation theory to study the low-energy behavior and found that, near the point of transition, the energy dispersion transitions smoothly from linear to parabolic. Our findings also demonstrate that, at the point of transition, the model's symmetry is significantly reduced compared to a Dirac semimetal in its conventional form. As a result, we propose that this novel model has the potential to be experimentally detected through a combination of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and electronic Raman spectroscopy.

We explore the entry and exit points of a nearly stable minimally supersymmetric topological defect in the M2/M5 system. To achieve this, we establish a mapping between the M2/M5 system and type 0A string theory and then examine how the defect's world-volume diagrams change as it enters and exits the AdS 4 region. Our work contributes to a broader understanding of how these high-energy states transition into the AdS 3 region.

Future third-generation gravitational-wave (GW) detectors are expected to surpass current sensitivity in various aspects, with some reaching into the advanced oscillation regime of GWs, specifically the tensor modes and vector gravitational waves. This advanced oscillation regime, which is typically associated with extremely high-frequency GWs, will introduce new complications in modeling GW propagation that have been overlooked in most current analyses. In this study, we examine the evolution of tensor and vector GWs in the third-generation era and find that the vector GW signal may persist for a longer duration than the tensor GW signal, potentially allowing for more accurate parameter measurements using the vector GW. We also discovered that the vector GW signal can partially counterbalance the loss of signal strength from the tensor GW due to its longer duration, potentially offsetting the negative impact of increased uncertainty in the tensor GW propagation time.

Astronomers have long been fascinated by the enigmatic "V-shape" in star systems, which can be a crucial indicator of the mass of the unseen companion. Using the astrometric data from Gaia Early Data Release 3, our study explores whether we can determine the mass of the Fomalhaut's companion, IKS J14005-4743, by measuring its gravitational influence on its host star. Our investigation reveals that, although the available data are limited, the gravitational interaction between the two stars is statistically significant, exceeding 14.4 standard deviations. This finding enables us to rule out various orbital configurations and, by assuming a specific orbit, we estimate that the companion's mass is approximately 0.58 times the mass of the Sun, with an error margin of 0.16. Our analysis demonstrates that, by leveraging partial astrometric data from Gaia, it is feasible to derive the masses of low-mass companions in the "V-shape" systems.

The 0/1 Knapsack problem is a significant NP-hard problem with extensive real-world significance, prompting the development of genetic algorithms as a solution approach. This study investigates the application of genetic algorithms with stochastic selection, one-point crossover, and modified order crossover techniques to tackle the maximum weight 0/1 Knapsack problem. This research aims to compare the efficacy of these three crossover techniques on random instances of the 0/1 Knapsack problem. Notably, the modified order crossover outperformed one-point crossover and yielded the fastest convergence time for the 0/1 Knapsack problem.

This paper is focused on the $L^2$ estimates of oscillatory integrals with three variables that have a convolution kernel, where the variables are part of $\mathbb{R}^2$. By introducing a new method of defining phase functions, we prove a general theorem for $L^2$ estimates. Additionally, our method can be used to derive $L^2$ estimates for oscillatory integrals with phases featuring non-degenerate critical points in two dimensions.

We examine the identification of hate speech in Arabic social media texts using the
latest pre-trained models. By the definition of ISO 3166, we are focusing on
instances of hate directed at national, ethnic, racial, religious, gender-based
groups, and political adversaries. Our research team developed an enhanced dataset
for identifying hate speech in Arabic, which is publicly available. We also
introduced a novel ensemble model combining the latest pre-trained models (T5,
GPT-2, XLNet), resulting in an 81.5% accuracy rate on the test data.

Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) research has extensively validated interactions for ions with fewer than ten nucleons, but extending this to heavier nuclei is a significant challenge. This problem is compounded by the computational burden of interaction calculations, particularly for complex configurations. We propose a novel approach to address this issue by developing a set of interaction approximations. These approximations are based on the observation that interactions within even-parity configurations are significantly more important than those in odd-parity configurations. By leveraging this odd-parity interaction, we can create a more efficient scaling model for even-parity configurations. We demonstrate that our approach yields a more robust scaling model for a wide range of interactions, including those based on universal and non-universal principles.

The 2020 US presidential election saw an unprecedented surge in allegations of election manipulation, particularly through social media platforms. By analyzing 1.7M tweets from both sides of the political spectrum, our study aimed to understand how false claims of election fraud spread and evolve over time, as well as their linguistic characteristics. Furthermore, our research explored the common threads between these false claims and their connections to broader online narratives. The findings of our investigation highlight the distinct strategies employed by the left and right sides of the political spectrum in promoting and adapting these false claims. The results also indicate a correlation between baseless election claims and the promotion of anti-democratic ideologies. The implications of our study emphasize the need for fact-checking to combat the spread of these false claims and maintain the integrity of the electoral process. The accompanying 'VoterDeception2020' dataset, which includes detailed information on the tweets analyzed, enables researchers to build upon our findings and advance the understanding of this complex issue.

We examine planar orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with a post-critical measure on $\mathbb{T}^2$, where the average eigenvalues, as per the Birkhoff normal form, are non-zero. In this context, we demonstrate the emergence of high-energy observables and the loss of regularity for the Koopman operator $U$.

Most deep learning applications for uncertainty estimation, particularly in fields like computer vision and robotics, require quantifying model uncertainty.  Traditional methods like Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) address this issue but are computationally expensive, limiting their real-world applicability due to the computational costs.  To improve the efficiency of uncertainty measurement in BNNs, we propose a new approach that combines the posterior distribution of BNNs with a new, compact representation technique.  Our method, inspired by the concept of forward-backward (FB) approximation in Markov chains, enables efficient computation of the posterior distribution.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by comparing it to other uncertainty measurement methods, such as Monte Carlo dropout and Variance-based approaches, on a variety of real-world computer vision tasks, showing promising results.

The Marcus-Levich-Jortner (MLJ) theory is a widely accepted concept in understanding the initial stages of charge transfer between molecules that are in non-equilibrium states. However, the underlying principles of MLJ are not explicitly stated in various implementations. In this work, we establish a theoretical basis for MLJ by utilizing the principles of quantum mechanics at strong coupling and applying a semiclassical approach. This allows us to demonstrate that the initial tunneling rate in quantum systems can be expressed as an activation process with an activation energy derived from instantons. Furthermore, by considering the effects of anharmonicity and adiabaticity, we show that the initial tunneling rate can be expressed as a function of exponential dependence on an effective barrier. This analysis enables us to identify and distinguish between the effects of instantons, anharmonicity, and adiabaticity on the tunneling rate. Our results are supported by numerical calculations using the multistate Tully model.

This paper presents a mixed approach for generating optimal guidance paths for linear target tracking systems. The proposed method combines a optimal control problem with a set of discrete guidance laws to create a mixed formulation. The resulting problem is reformulated as a mixed-integer linear programming problem and solved using advanced optimization algorithms, which offers superior guidance compared to traditional optimal control and rule-based methods. The proposed method is particularly effective in scenarios involving constrained or limited path areas.

A significant thermoelectric phenomenon, the vast thermoelectric effect, is being explored for its potential to achieve high efficiency. This research develops a microscopic understanding of its thermodynamic and magnetic properties in a magnetic insulator, specifically the Co$_{2}$FeGa Heusler alloy. By analyzing the behavior of magnons, electronic holes, and electrons under thermal and magnetic influences, it was discovered that the VTE's efficiency is influenced by the competition between the spin-flip energy of magnons and the Schottky energy of charge carriers. This concept may also apply to other materials. Computational simulations of the Co$_{2}$FeGa alloy suggest that the VTE's efficiency can reach up to 20% at a certain temperature range, which could be enhanced by adjusting the magnetic properties of the material.

This research focuses on the ideal sum problem, which seeks to determine whether a given integer can be expressed as the sum of two squares with specific modular properties. By developing a probabilistic algorithm based on repeated trials, we demonstrate that the ideal sum problem can be solved in a time complexity of $O(\sqrt{N} \log^{3.5k} (3.5k \sqrt{N}))$. Furthermore, our approach is applied to a related mathematical problem known as the Beal Conjecture.

We present a method for calculating the factorization of polynomials of degree n, specifically those of the form $f(x) = x^n + \alpha$, within finite fields of size $q = p^t$, where $p$ is a prime number, $t$ is a positive integer, and $\alpha$ is a non-square root. This method is computationally efficient and can be completed in $O(t)$ multiplications among the elements of the field. The process involves the sequential factorization of simpler polynomials of the form $x^n + bp^j$, with $b$ being a fixed coefficient, from which we derive the final result. To validate the method's efficacy, we provide an example of a high-degree polynomial over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{13}$, specifically $f(x) = x^{10} + 2$, and verify that it requires 5 multiplications. Furthermore, we also describe an alternative, simplified procedure for calculating the partial products of the individual factors of $f(x)$.

In software development, code analysis is a critical process, and code analysis tools play a vital role in ensuring efficient project delivery in accordance with predefined requirements. Our research focuses on examining source code through the UPPAAL tool, which allows us to verify code compliance with specified constraints, evaluate the impact of code modifications, compare the efficiency of similar codes, and determine the adequacy of test cases. This paper outlines the practical application of UPPAAL in these scenarios and provides specific instructions for users.

Recent research has demonstrated the feasibility of using radio frequency enabled metasurfaces for imaging applications. Despite their potential, actual implementations have fallen short of the ideal performance due to various limitations, necessitating ongoing advancements in metasurfaces. This study focuses on the enhancement of a metasurface system, originally developed using an evolutionary algorithm, through an in-depth analysis of its performance metrics. Building upon this foundation, an integrated method is proposed that combines the compressed sensing framework with the evolutionary algorithm for enhanced imaging capabilities. This approach is validated through a series of simulations and is expected to contribute to the ongoing development and improvement of metasurface-based imaging systems.
Using a three-step ionization process, we explain the occurrence of Stark-displaced resonances observed in intense circularly polarized laser fields with two frequencies.

This paper investigates the challenge of generating an image blend composition that aligns with the underlying content's semantic structure. The generation of image blends is typically viewed as a straightforward task, as it involves merging two images based on an alpha mask. However, we argue that this conventional approach underestimates the intricacies of image blends and the expected semantic outcomes. In contrast, we treat image blend composition as a specific instance of the image condensation task, where we aim to condense an image into a compact, semantically interpretable form. To this end, we propose a novel framework that reimagines image blend creation by replacing predefined regions with semantic components derived from a pre-trained language-image model. These semantic components are then used to refine the image blend's structure. The resulting approach enables the creation of image blends that not only have a visually pleasing alpha mask but also are more effectively understood by humans and machines alike.

The regulation of gene expression is inherently a stochastic process. Researchers use a spatially spatially implicit (SI) model to simulate this noise, which is informed by a chemical Langevin equation and adheres to the laws of thermodynamics. To extract meaningful information from these simulations, we employ a variational autoencoder, a type of generative adversarial network, to capture the SI model's latent space. Our approach enables the calculation of key statistics such as the distribution of protein copies in cells and the correlation between adjacent cells. Additionally, we utilize our variational model to determine whether experimental data exhibit unusual patterns, and apply it to a well-known dataset on the human immune response to a viral infection.

A computer vision approach inspired by educational learning is introduced, where student images are categorized into clusters based on their semi-supervised learning. The algorithm is educated by assigning cluster centers that serve as additional labels, gradually refining cluster definitions as it progresses. Inspired by this framework, a data-driven semi-supervised approach utilizing the StyleGAN framework is developed to generate high-quality images from limited labels. The algorithm is evaluated on the CelebA dataset under various settings, demonstrating its effectiveness in combining the advantages of semi-supervised and self-supervised learning methods.

A widely used heuristic to find low-energy states in quantum many-body systems is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Problem (QAOCCenter). This approach involves solving optimization problems with variational quantum circuits, whose architecture is divided into layers, and each layer is optimized separately using a local, unconstrained optimization method. This method, however, has a significant issue - it causes the circuit to become overly complex and lose its generalisation ability when it goes beyond what the training data can handle. This problem, referred to as 'overloading', is particularly severe in the QAOA method, especially when it comes to handling complex combinatorial optimization problems like the MaxCut. This issue is explored in the context of the MaxCut problem, where it is shown that overloading can be detected by monitoring the increasing coherence between different states in the output layer of the circuit, which can occur when it goes beyond what the training data can handle. This issue is also shown to be mitigated by reducing the coherence between different states in the output layer of the circuit.

We are tackling the complex challenge of identifying individuals within datasets, particularly hospital records, even with de-identified data. The security risks associated with unmasking the identities of patients within these datasets are significant. The existing research on the unmasking of anonymous medical data has largely been confined to the analysis of the unmasking of individual records within databases. Conversely, our research delves into the unmasking of anonymous medical data at the individual level. Our proposed framework involves a straightforward, efficient, and effective method of unmasking that draws on the concept of minimizing the differential entropy of anonymous data. The proposed method involves a straightforward, efficient, unmasking strategy that incorporates a novel, two-stage, entropy-based optimization function. The optimization problem is solved using the differential evolution algorithm. The effectiveness of our proposed unmasking approach has been evaluated through a series of experiments involving both simulated and real-world datasets. The evaluation of our unmasking approach has demonstrated that it offers superior performance compared to the existing methods. The results of our unmasking approach have significant implications for the security and protection of anonymous medical data.

To advance power systems restoration research, we provide open-access data from real-world events that have been thoroughly documented with expert insights and analytical results. This contribution is part of a broader movement towards sharing and utilizing domain-specific data that facilitates scientific discovery. The provided data are specifically tailored to address power systems restoration challenges, offering a comprehensive, multi-faceted approach. The data set encompasses a variety of restoration scenarios, offering a rich source of information for both research and validation efforts. The diverse nature of the data, including scenarios such as storms and cyber-attacks, allows researchers to explore and analyze different scenarios, including both normal and extreme conditions. The data is made available to facilitate research into domain-specific problems, including the optimal placement of distributed energy resources, and to foster a deeper understanding of real-world phenomena. The data set is accompanied by in-depth guidance and tools to ensure seamless usage, providing a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field.

We investigate a modified iterative scheme, originally designed to derive error estimates for the strong convergence of its iterative sequence to the sole solution of a given variational inequality problem. Our analysis reveals that removing an initial step from the algorithm yields a robust convergence result, one that remains unaffected by the presence of additive noise or monotone perturbations within the underlying equation, as well as any convexity conditions that may apply. A key demonstration of this approach is achieved through the analysis of a second-order optimality condition.

Following the guidance of Cross, we examine the structure of sign patterns in hyperbolic triangles formed by geodesic crossings, with a focus on groups classified as isoxial Fuchsian groups. Our method involves applying topological principles to present these groups in terms of triangular surfaces and then determining their respective triangle sets. We also investigate the characteristics of these sets in various cases and illustrate our findings with specific examples from the triangle set of $H_4$.

The process $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ has been studied to investigate lepton flavor violation. The branching ratio for this process has been calculated using perturbative quantum chromodynamics, yielding a result of $2.73\times10^{-10}$. Comparisons were made with current experimental limits and other theoretical predictions. Our analysis suggests that future experiments may have the potential to detect $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e\mu$ and $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e\mu$, provided they can achieve sensitivities of $10^{-10}$ or better.

The Kagome lattice structure, found in various metals, presents a unique platform for studying flat-band superconductivity. Research has shown that flat-band superconductivity is feasible in certain materials, yet evidence is lacking for many others. Our study reveals that the compound Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ (PPSSe) meets the flat-band requirement near its Fermi level, and exhibits a pressure-driven transformation of normal-state behavior from non-superconducting to superconducting, then to non-superconducting again. The superconducting state's characteristics remain consistent with a s-wave pairing scenario, while the pressure-induced transition is linked to a topological phase transition. Our findings provide substantial evidence for the occurrence of flat-band superconductivity in PPs and demonstrate the potential of utilizing chemical pressure as a means to explore this phenomenon in other Kagome materials.

We have developed a method for extracting gravitational wave data from the quantum gravity model of Jackiw-Teitelboth, using a quantum effective action that describes a 2d dilaton gravity with negative curvature. Our approach involves calculating the probability of a specific configuration in the quantum state by integrating over the corresponding phase space volume. We found that the expected value of relevant observables in the vacuum state is zero unless the boundary conditions are specified, in which case it can be positive, satisfying the energy condition. Furthermore, we have derived a method for calculating the expected value of gravitational wave data in the vacuum state, using the boundary conditions as a variable, and have shown that the data approaches the classical prediction for a specific value of the boundary condition. We also compared our results with the analysis of boundary conditions by using the Fock basis and found a similar result.

Neural ODEs have become a popular choice in learning complex dynamics due to their ability to handle irregular and noisy data from systems that are affected by hidden factors. However, existing methods often assume that measurement errors follow a pattern over time, which may not always be the case. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method that leverages neural networks to efficiently model non-stationary systems with time-variant, noisy and erratic data. By using a hidden process to generate the observed data, we can estimate this process along with the system dynamics and the neural network parameters. To ensure the model's identifiability, we incorporate a total variation constraint that prevents the learned hidden process from having excessive complexity. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness in achieving superior performance compared to existing approaches under various noise conditions.

The Object Target Navigation challenge in robotics and AI requires guiding an agent to a specific target object within an unorganized space with numerous objects. Most current approaches model the environment as a point cloud and use a single query to determine the target, but these methods often fail in complex scenarios involving multiple objects in view. In this research, we introduce a novel transformer-based OTN architecture that effectively handles the object recall problem by utilizing a memory bank to store and recall object features. We also propose a distinct target prediction method using a region proposal network and a classification head, and we experiment with different memory bank update strategies. We evaluate our model's performance on the OTN dataset and achieve superior results compared to previous methods, particularly in complex scenarios with multiple objects in view.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of fine-tuning language models on instruction-based meta learning. Current research has primarily focused on optimizing these models' performance on specific tasks. This work, instead, explores how instruction meta learning can enhance generalization. We introduce OPT-IML, a family of models, to examine the impact of pretraining and fine-tuning techniques on generalization. An extensive empirical evaluation was conducted, which revealed that smaller models benefit from extensive pretraining and that instruction diversity enhances fine-tuning performance. Notably, our analysis found that OPT-IML can achieve competitive results with significantly fewer parameters.

Children's technology skills develop over time through extended use, but creating opportunities for them to explore various roles and systems can help them build skills and confidence in technology faster. Peripheral participation, a concept introduced by Lave and Wenger, refers to temporary engagement with a community of practice, offering limited yet valuable contributions and benefiting from the community's knowledge and expertise. This study investigates the peripheral participation of novice users in Scratch, a popular platform enabling users to create and share creative computing experiences.
